**All 14 assertions linked to I1 (Hermann Gaetjen, husband of Amelia Nichols) — but at "speculative" confidence.**

### Links created

| Source | Assertions | Linked to | Confidence | Score |
|--------|-----------|-----------|------------|-------|
| src_001 (1875 SF Great Register) | a_001–a_009 | I1 | speculative | 0.43 |
| src_002 (Germans to America Index) | a_010–a_014 | I1 | speculative | 0.006 |

No stub person was created — both records describe a single consistent individual (b. ~1854, Prussia/Germany, arriving NY 1871, in San Francisco by 1875) who matches I1's circumstantial profile too closely to treat as a separate person.

---

### Why speculative, not higher

**Core conflict:** Both records give birth ~1854; I1's tree entry has an unsourced estimate of ~1859 — a 5-year gap. Because I1's birth year carries no evidentiary weight (it is unsourced), two independent government records versus a tree guess should resolve in favor of ~1854, but that decision must go through **conflict-resolution** first.

**Naturalization shortfall:** Arrival 2 Jun 1871 → naturalization 13 Aug 1875 is only ~4 years 2 months, slightly short of the required 5 years. This is a secondary flag worth investigating.

---

### Why both records were assigned to I1 (not a stub)

The two other known Hermann Gaetjens in California are firmly excluded:
- Born 1873 — too young to father children in 1878.
- Born 1827, died 1899 in Butte County — wrong era and location.

No other candidate exists. The 1875 San Francisco placement fits perfectly (Henry Joseph was born in SF in 1878). Creating a stub would almost certainly manufacture a duplicate.

---

### Recommended next step

Run **conflict-resolution** to weigh the two evidenced birth years (~1854 from both records) against the unsourced ~1859 tree estimate. Resolving in favor of ~1854 will upgrade these links to `probable`, allow facts (Prussia origin, SF address, naturalization date) to materialize onto I1's tree entry, and open the door to answering the research question about when and from where in Germany (Prussia) Hermann Gaetjen immigrated.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The 1913 San Francisco marriage record of Amelia Gaetjen and William Fralich has now been fully matched to the family. The bride was confirmed as the same Amelia Otillie Gaetjen already in the family tree. Her stated parents — Hermann Gaetjen and Amelia Nichols — were very confidently identified as I1 and I4 (scores of 0.97 and 0.96 respectively). quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The 1913 San Francisco marriage record of Amelia Gaetjen and William Fralich has now been fully matched to the family. The bride, confirmed as the same Amelia Otillie Gaetjen already in the family tree, stated that her father was Hermann Gaetjen and her mother was Amelia Nichols — both very likely identified as the same Hermann and Amelia already in the tree (scores of 0.97 and 0.96 respectively), with both other local Hermann Gaetjens firmly ruled out: one died in 1899 and could not appear in a 1913 record, and the other born in 1873 would have been only ten years old when Amelia was born in 1883. The next step is to use this confirmed family connection as corroboration when proof-conclusion assembles the answer to when and from where in Germany Hermann immigrated.

**Linking and Tree Updates**

All seven census assertions (a_001–a_007) were processed. Thomas Flynn (I2), the household head, was confirmed as the anchor. Two new tree persons were created:

- **John Flynn** (I3) — son, born ~1842 in Ireland
- **Bridget Flynn** (I4) — daughter, born ~1844 in Ireland

Birth facts and name facts from the census were written onto each new person's tree record, and parent-child relationships connecting both to Thomas were created. Eight new person_evidence links (pe_002–pe_009) were recorded.

**Notable Absence: Patrick Flynn (I1)**

Patrick, already in the tree as Thomas's son born ~1845, does **not** appear in this 1850 census household. The agent flagged several possible explanations:

1. He may not yet have been born by June 1850 (pushing his estimated birth later than currently recorded).
2. He may have died before the enumeration.
3. He may have been living elsewhere at the time.
4. This could potentially be a different Thomas Flynn household (though the name, county, and Irish origin align).

This absence should be investigated before the household reconstruction is considered complete. If you'd like to explore it further — checking Patrick's dates, building a timeline, or resolving the discrepancy — just let me know.

Both warnings are pre-existing advisory issues (severity: implausible) about "Ireland" not being linked to a standard place on the Birth facts of I2 and I1. These preceded this run and no new impossibilities were introduced.

---

Here is what was done with the 1850 census of Thomas Flynn's household:

Thomas Flynn (already in the tree) was confirmed as the household head across three assertions — his name assertion was already linked by pe_001, and the two relationship assertions (child_1-to-head and child_2-to-head) were now linked to him as well (pe_005 and pe_009). Two new family members were discovered in this census and added to the tree: John Flynn, Thomas's son born roughly 1842 in Ireland (now person I3), and Bridget Flynn, a daughter born roughly 1844 in Ireland (now person I4). Their birth and name facts from the census were written onto their new tree records, and two parent-child relationships connecting them to Thomas were created. All told, eight new person_evidence links were recorded (pe_002 through pe_009), and all three personas were matched or minted — none left dangling.

One notable absence: Patrick Flynn, who is already in the tree as Thomas's son born roughly 1845, does not appear anywhere in this 1850 census household. At age five he should have been listed if present. This could mean he had not yet been born by the June 1850 census date (which would push his birth a bit later than estimated), that he died before the enumeration, that he was living elsewhere with another family member, or that this is an entirely different Thomas Flynn household — though the name, county, and Irish origin all align with the research objective. This question needs an answer before the household reconstruction can be considered complete.

**Summary in plain terms:**

Two sources were evaluated for Hermann Gaetjen. The **1875 San Francisco voter registration** (src_001, a_001–a_009) is very likely the right person — he gave his address as 5 Cook Street, the exact same address where a Hermann Gaetjen appears in the 1869 city directory already on file — but the age he reported (21) puts his birth around 1854, while the family tree currently says "about 1859" with no source. Because those two birth years disagree, the matching rule requires leaving the connection as only *speculative* until that discrepancy is resolved; once it is, his birthplace (Germany), naturalization date (13 Aug 1875), and occupation (fireman) will transfer automatically to his tree record.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

"Herm" is almost certainly an index truncation of "Hermann"; the underlying manifest's spelling cannot be verified without the original record. Identity of this passenger with tree subject I1 (Hermann Gaetjen, born ~1859) is uncertain: the stated birth year 1854 differs from the tree subject's approximate birth year by five years. This identity question must be resolved by corroborating evidence, not asserted from this index alone.

Birth year 1854 as stated in the index conflicts with the tree subject I1's approximate birth year of ~1859 — a five-year discrepancy that raises an identity question. Notably, the 1875 San Francisco Great Register entry (src_001) records a Hermann Gatjen aged 21, implying birth ~1854, which is consistent with this index entry; the two may record the same individual. Whether that individual is the same as tree subject I1 requires independent corroboration. The birth year in a passenger index would typically derive from the passenger's self-reported age or a birth year column on the original manifest; neither can be verified without the original.

Prussia is a broad political designation covering a large territory, not a specific locality. It does not identify a German province, town, or parish of origin. The index records no departure port or ship name, so the original manifest — which may carry a more specific origin — cannot be located from this entry alone.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

---

Searching for a William Weller passenger record crossing from England to America in the 1860s is the recommended next step.
